facts.statement: In fruit flies, a protein called Sex Peptide transferred from males makes mated females sleep less during the day and eat more than females that have not mated.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: P2 neurons were chosen for study because they produce a hormone linked to eating and sleeping, connect directly to the fly's main sleep control area, and are known to change sleep and eating habits when flies are isolated.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The researchers used a genetic tool to either turn on or turn off the P2 neurons in both mated and unmated female flies.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Sleep time was tracked with activity monitors, and food intake was measured using capillary feeder devices and a blue-dye method.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The study found that changing the activity of P2 neurons did not stop mated females from sleeping less and eating more than unmated females.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The results suggest that P2 neurons are probably not the main brain cells that process the male protein to control post-mating sleep and eating changes.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The authors note that future research is needed to see if these neurons control other behaviors after mating or affect sleep and eating only in specific situations.
facts.subject: animals
